Sumimi v0.4.2 — **the memory of a request, cut by a third**.

**What this is.** A week of measuring where a request's memory goes, and
seven changes that take it away. The request path allocates 12% less, and the
peak resident set — the number the 512 MB promise is about — drops at every
rate from 20 000 requests a second up.

**What was wrong.** Not one thing but seven, and the biggest was not where
anyone would have guessed:

* **The queue moved every hit in it.** Growing a `VecDeque` copies the whole
  queue, so the longer the queue was, the more each request allocated — and
  the queue's length is exactly what the traffic rate decides. A push into a
  queue of 1 000 rows cost **10 331 bytes**; into the new one, **1 054**.
* **There was no batch.** The writer only waited when the queue was empty, so
  one request was usually one DuckDB transaction. Now it waits for a full
  batch: 1 000 requests are 3 transactions, not 1 000.
* **The payload was a tree.** The body was parsed into a `serde_json::Value`
  tree, copied into a map, and every field copied out of it again. Now it is
  parsed straight into the fields the collector reads — **697 bytes** of tree
  per request became **49**.
* **The channel lookup lowercased the referrer once per domain.** There are
  over a hundred domains in the list, and each of them lowercased the referrer
  again: **1 731 bytes per request**, spent on the same string, a hundred
  times over. The needles are lowercase constants and the referrer is
  lowercased once now, so the whole lookup allocates nothing.
* **The fields were copied instead of moved** into the event, and the
  allocator kept the pages it took instead of giving them back.

**The numbers.** The first table is the counting allocator in the test suite
(the release build); the second is the peak, measured end to end on an Apple
M5 with the released binary, before and after:

| one request | before | after |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| the body, parsed | 697 B | **49 B** |
| building the event | 3 493 B | **898 B** |
| the whole request | 26 347 B | **23 128 B** |
| a push into a queue of 1 000 rows | 10 331 B | **1 054 B** |

| the rate offered | before (v0.4.1) | after (v0.4.2) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 5 000 /s | 104 MB | 120 MB |
| 10 000 /s | 123 MB | 123 MB |
| 20 000 /s | 227 MB | 227 MB |
| 40 000 /s | 287 MB | **249 MB** |

The low rates are the price of the batching: the batch waits in memory until
it is written, so it is memory the server holds on purpose. The default is
now **1 000 rows** instead of 10 000, which is what the table above uses;
`SUMIMI_MAX_BATCH` changes it.

**Nothing changed for the user.** The API takes the same bodies, the tracker
still works, the reports say the same things — and every field the tracker
sends is still read (`service/tests/tracker.rs` checks that the two ends
agree, field for field). The rules that decide a visit's channel are the
same rules, in the same order.

**One thing to set.** `MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_=65536` in the environment file
tells glibc to give the pages back when it frees a large block instead of
keeping them for later. The Docker image already sets it; a systemd
deployment should add it — it is worth **23% of the peak**:

| the allocator | the peak |
| --- | ---: |
| the default | 274 MB |
| `MALLOC_MMAP_THRESHOLD_=65536` | **210 MB** |

| Linux (ARM64) | `sumimi-v0.4.2-Linux-aarch64.tar.gz` |

Unpack it and run it:

```bash
sumimi serve --dir ./sumimi --port 3000
```
